Grup de fete și feciori îmbrăcați în costume populare tradiționale din zona Banat. Fetele poartă cămașă încrețită la gât și mâneci lungi și largi, vestă descheiată în față cu decorații, poale, șort cu broderii și aplicații de dantelă în partea de jos. Bărbații au pe cap pălării și sunt îmbrăcați cu cămașă largă cu mâneci lungi, pantaloni albi largi, peste cămașă au o vestă descheiată cu mai multe rânduri de nasturi. În picioare poartă cizme. Fotografia este făcută lângă un perete al gospodărie. Pe carton, în partea de jos, însemnări manuscrise cu tuș negru: ”Glogon în 15 August 1903 / Fete și feciori din Glogon (Banat) / Theodor Filipescu chimist”. În partea de sus, stânga, urme de lipire / dezlipire de pe un alt suport. Pe verso însemnări manuscrise cu creion, ștampilă incomplet vizibilă "Muzeul "Brukenthal" Sibiu / Nr. 14.365" (cifră scrisă cu cerneală și tăiată); număr inventar MCPR 563.

R: Grup de șase femei îmbrăcate în port popular de sărbătoare din Banatul sârbesc. Fotografie de exterior, realizată în fața unui arbore. Fotografia este lipită de o hârtie de culoare crem. V: Pe verso însemnări manuscrise în creion ("Banat / Ofcea / 277 ASTRA / Col. ASTRA 1905 / Catal. I B 57"), însemnare manuscrisă cu stiloul "Port femeiesc din Ofcea - Comint. Timiș-Torantal / Cercul Panciova / Foto ing. Th. Filipescu, 10 august 1903", ștampilă "Muzeul "Brukenthal" Sibiu / Nr. 14.306" (cifră scrisă cu cerneală și tăiată); număr inventar MCPR 512.

Fotografia de interior realizată în expoziția permanentă a Muzeului Secuiesc din Șumuleu Ciuc (actualmente cartier al localității Miercurea Ciuc), județul Harghita. Imaginea este imprimată pe hârtie fotografică cu gelatino-bromură de argint (Gelatin Silver Print). Reprezintă o femeie în costum popular secuiesc, lucrând la un război de țesut. Se remarcă războiul orizontal și textilele expuse pe pereții încăperii. Fotografia este lipită pe un carton gri, parte a albumului realizat în 1930. Acesta cuprinde imagini din expoziție și piesele expuse. Sub fotografie, număr de inventar MCPR 1392 și text în limba maghiară, imprimat pe o bucată de hârtie albă: „Szekely szövőasszony” (Țesătoare din secuime).

Portrait of a man (named Ah-fit-che, better known as Pedro Jose Quivera), the governor of San Felipe pueblo, sitting on a blanket, demonstrating the use of a pump-drill, a tool used to drill holes in flat turquoise and shell beads.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), 'the point of the drill is a small flake of flint fastened in a slit in the lower end of the shaft which is tightly wrapped either with a string or sinew.  When the stone point becomes dull it is sharpened by flaking the tip in the same manner that flint arrow points are made.  The wheel is made sometimes of stone, wood, or bone, the former being preferable.  The piece of turquois[e] to be drilled is placed in a suitable cavity in a block of wood and held there by the thumb of the left hand while the drill is manipulated by the right, as shown in the picture.  Turquois[e] and shell bead drilling is extensively practised by the Indians of the Rio Grande valley.'

A section of vegetation or gardens, possibly including a planted ?fruit tree, with a homestead in the background. Judging by the original film number there is the possibility that this is part of Pirgwinyo village in eastern Anuakland.

A view of sparse savannah vegetation with the huts of a village beyond, possibly just beyond a dried river-bed (darker colour), possibly Pochala or near Pochala?. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during March-May this image shows the savannah at the beginning of the rainy season.

A carrier walking past baggage (including a rifle and shotgun) laid on the ground during a break in the day's march across Anuakland. Evans-Pritchard notes that he was able to recruit Anuak porters locally in Akobo at the beginning of the two month expedition in March 1935.
A portrait of a seated young man with other youths craning their necks to see the camera, under the shelter of a large canvas tent put up by Evans-Pritchard at Pochala.

Large tufts of grass leading up to a derelict stockade of branches stuck in the ground surrounding the huts of Dibango village, and in front of that a shallow ditch or moat, constructed in the past as a form of defence against raids.
Looking along the path ahead through grass savannah a woman carries a gourd vessel on her head, possibly returning from a pool or well nearby.

A girl in Pochala village bending down showing a handful of flour from a gourd vessel, with a long wooden pestle to pound grain (probably millet) in a sunken mortar next to her. A grass brush for keeping the area around the mortar clean is nearby.
A view through trees towards the expanse of flood water known as Oleng on the Akobo river south of Pochala.

Dance rattle, made from 37 small, spherical gourds strung onto a long piece of plant fibre rope. Each gourd has a hole through the middle and a tube, possibly of cane, has been inserted into the hole. This prevents the seeds that are inside the gourd from falling out. The gourds are threaded onto a long piece of plant fibre rope, which is presumably how the rattle would be operated. Some of the gourds are cracked and damaged, and there is an additional gourd that is detached but present.

A wooden drum, squat and cylindrical, with a stepped base that is narrower than the body. A skin is stretched over the top and down the sides, where is is held in place with wooden pegs. There is a small hole in each side, through which a plant fibre rope is threaded.

Belt of buffalo skin, with three cartridge pouches attached (one of which is made of the skin of an elephant's ear, one is closed with a red glass bead toggle). Both the belt and two of the pouches are decorated with stamped ornament. Belt secured with a small metal buckle.

Large, sub-rectangular, dark brown piece of barkcloth with black patterning on one side and patches of similar barkcloth stitched in. The central pattern consist of spots in concentric circles, organised into four vertical rectangles separated by double lines. The central pattern is bordered on the long edges by narrow rectangles that are divided into triangles and filled with dots and crescents. The design is wholly bordered by straight lines forming concentric rectangles, which are filled with dots and diagonal lines.

Wili sape. Knife. Iron, double-edged blade with wooden handle wrapped in brass wire. Leather sheath with tip and mouth wrapped in flat copper wire. Used for shaving and other small purposes. Often is a payment in ceremonial exchange or purchase. Wili sape.

Iron knife with two double-edged blades either side of a rectangular grip bound with copper wire. Both blades are decorated on both faces along the central ridge with incised ornamentation in zig-zags or nicks. Possibly for shaving.

An iron knife with a broad sickle shaped blade and a wooden haft. The shoulders are at different heights with the cutting edge side being lower. At the base of the blade are two circular perforations. The narrow tang is fitted into a cylindrical wooden haft, partially bound in wire; it has a wider cylindrical terminal.
gbina mbipo. Trap for catching pigeons. Consisting of a dark twisted fibre net suspended between two wooden sticks. Each stick has a pointed end with traces of soil, possibly caused from use.
Ngaka or agba. Skirt made from long strips of banana leaves plaited over a broad waistband.

A piled arrangement on a table (probably in front of a fence) of Zande carved wooden bowls and stools, as well as a throwing knife placed in front. It is possible that Buchta collected a number of Zande objects on his brief expedition to this part of Sudan. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

A tuka or spirit shrine in a garden, showing a split stick, the ends bound at the top and a ritual offering in the split of the stick and on the ground below. Such shrines are sites for medicines or ngua that are invoked to ensure ancestral spirit (atoro) favour for the garden.

A gathering of abinza (witchdoctors) held in Evans-Pritchard's own compound on the occasion of the initiation of a new member, Evans-Pritchard's servant Kamanga, which facilitated the gathering of data on the abinza corporation. They are dancing around a hole being dug for the ritual 'burial' of the initiate.
A standing group of four boys of varying ages, one wearing shorts, two others small loincloths (bagadi)

A binza (identified as Kamanga) standing in a homestead in full dancing apparel, including headdress. Kamanga was initiated in the abinza corporation at the instigation of Evans-Pritchard in order to gain ethnographic information about the corporation's medicines and ritual practices.

A woman with heavy cicatrisation on her chest making "eyes" as a joke during the ritual anointment of widows at the termination of their mourning period, when a feast is held. Since she is wearing a man's brimmed straw hat (kisikindi), she may well be comically acting out the new attentions of men towards the widows who are free to remarry.

Major P. M. Larken, the District Commissioner for Yambio District (1911-1932), sitting on the ground with his arm around a girl, with a boy next to them. In front of them is a carved stool, and in the background a sleeping hut (type known as gbuguru).

The Lotuko rain-maker Ikang (left) with a companion, standing in front of a tall conical hut. Ikang was the widow of three earlier rain-makers and was held in high esteem by locals. The Seligmans visited Lotuko country in the early part of 1922, and according to their diary they travelled between these villages by bicycle.

A three-quarter length portrait of two Mandari youths dancing, with arms gesturing in imitation of the training of the horn of their favourite ox [partial double exposure at top]. The training of ox horns for aesthetically pleasing effects is carried out by most Nilotic cattle-keeping groups. One arm is curved forwards in imitation of the training of the left horn across the muzzle. The other arm curves upwards and to one side. The youth to the right is also wearing the waist string beads of a particular age set.

A three-quarter length group portrait of a youth and a girl wearing a checked waist-cloth, with other youths standing in a line beside them. She is wearing a number of beads around her neck, probably given to her by male admirers such as the youth standing beside her. She and the youths to her left have also prominent forehead scarification after the manner of the Dinka, although for the Mandari it does not denote any formal initiation (hence her use of it along with the youths), and was used instead for aesthetically pleasing effect.

An upper body portrait of a Mandari girl wearing strings of beads around neck. Girls often wore beads given to them by male admirers, but they did not indicate any age sets or grades amongst the women. She also has scarification patterns on her forehead after the manner of the nearby Dinka, as well as decorative lines on her abdomen. These did not indicate any initiation procedure however but were done for aesthetically pleasing effect only.
A full length group image of five young Mandari women wearing textile body cloths, standing in a homestead. One of them is smoking a pipe.

A full length portrait of a Mandari man wearing a thick and expensive ivory arm ornament, with three boys (probably sons) in their homestead, standing next to two wooden shrine stakes (ködi lo jok). The family would sometimes make offerings to such shrines to spiritual powers, for instance after diagnosis by a Mandari doctor regarding illness caused by a malevolent spirit. The shrine stake thereby stands for the presence of a spirit within the family dwelling.

Three caryatid stools, a carved figure and an iron staff. The caryatid figures of the stools represent animals (leopards?). The  male figure, which holds a human head in his left hand and a calabash (?) in his right, is identified as a commemorative figure for fon Tshakutio de Bazou. The figure wears a necklace as well as a necklace around the hips. The eyes and teeth of the figure are accentuated by white pigment. The figure is also represented with a cap. The iron staff in the nearer foreground to the right shows twisted branches which partly end up in leaflike forms. Houses in the background (see also 1998.112.20).

Two caryatid stools, one standing on top as the other. The one standing on the ground is the same as on 199.110.59. The caryatid stool on top of that stool shows anthropomorphic figures as caryatid figures. The rim of the upper stool is decorated with geometric patterns. The base of the upper stool is badly damaged by insect bites (?). The stools are standing in front of a house entrance (see 1998.110.59).

Women and girls in the Elbola gorge collecting water with scoops so that they can see any leeches there might be in the water. Note the frames, sakapa, for carrying the gourds.
Pêcheurs rentrant du lac Victoria chez eux

This is a scene of bull fighting where mature bulls fight it out to determine who controls the heard, particularly the cows. The bull owner also takes the clan and village pride of having the powerful bull and musicians can sing praises of him. The herd is seen to the side. The location could be Nyanza, but not necessarily Luo country. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]
A view of Uyoma village in Alego Location, with a number of homesteads (mier) visible in the open and shrubby landscape. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A small antelope photographed on a path. It is a source of excellent meat for hunters and its horns were made into musical instruments. Most of the Luo blown musical instruments are made out of this deer's horn, particularly the side-blown deer horn (tung or ndweru). Deer skulls and horns are also used in some rituals,such as for boats (see ritual adornment of the Kadimo boat in 1998.349.185 and the Kendu Bay boat 1998.349.217). [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A view of Luo country from a hillside, with a man in the foreground leaning on a stick. He is standing next to a substantial stone boundary wall (ohinga) which can be seen curving away to the right. This may be Alego or Ugenya Location. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 16/03/2007]

This is the landscape of the area around Kendu Bay in Karachuonyo Location, South Nyanza District. The terrain drops away from the hills above Kendu Bay into the open flat land towards the shore, with Lake Victoria seen in the far background. This is a densely settled area and Luo homesteads can be seen below, often spread out as groups of fenced homesteads with grass thatch huts, surrounded by thick euphorbia fences. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A school group in front of their classroom at Kagonya village school in Ugenya. The school building is a distinctive long rectangular grass thatch building divided into single rooms, possibly up to five classes. The children's shirts have a distinctive badge incorporating the letters 'SK' which may be a reference to the school name. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

A group of six  schoolchildren of Mulaha School posed for a photograph, one wearing the badge of the school on his uniform, a cross on a shield. It seems likely that they are posed like this due to the visit of Evans-Pritchard and his host Archdeacon Owen. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004 & CM 23/03/2007]

This man is sitting on a wooden chair outside his grass thatch hut. He is clean shaved using an iron blade (nyamarich) except a small patch on top center of his head, He has an ostrich eggshell necklace (rek) and glass bead earrings of the type worn by men (ngaga). His clothing is simply of animal (cow?) skin (pien), which was a common Luo attire. Beyond him, looking back toward the camera is another man dressed in colonial service clothing. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

This is a section of the Sondu River between Nyakach and Kabondo Locations in South Nyanza District. The Sondu River starts in the Nandi and Kipsigis highlands and flows down through the steep gorges of Nyakach and Kabondo Hills and into Lake Victoria in the southern part of Kavirondo (Winam) Gulf. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

An old DIRI drum sits on the ground, images of footprints all around. The DIRI drum is a special form of  medium sized drum, used solely for funerals. When someone died they used to beat the drum. It is made of WERE wood, with a pigskin (wild boar) cover and hide fronds which are plaited around it. In Deborah's (informant) compound. Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

This is a side view of a winnowing tray, KUBI, made with DURA fronds from the stem of the sorghum (durrha) plant. Small fronds make an intricate weave, with coloured fronds interwoven. In Deborah's (informant) compound. Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

A top view of a meat pot, MOLA, sits on the ground in Deborah (informant's) compound. This is a medium sized meat pot. It has a plain rim and cross-hatched body. MOLA is the correct name (not Moya as in the primary documentation) Patti Langton [16/03/2009]

In this image, informant Deborah's mother stands in front of her sleeping hut, ZO. The exterior mud has been washed off and not replaced leaving the skeleton exposed. As an elderly widow, it is likely she will have to wait for a younger family member to help her to repair the hut. Deborah's mother has a number of houses to tend, as she has children living in Juba and Maridi. They have their village house also. To the right of the mother's sleeping hut, a hut is hidden by a high fence. This is where Deborah's daughter recently gave birth. The baby is now 3 weeks old. The reason given for the fence was to "prevent wind affecting the birth". Birth is followed by 4-7 days' seclusion. A bed of logs is located to the right of Deborah's mother's hut and a large pot, LUKUDU, sits in the centre of the compound (probably to be photographed). Patti Langton [23/03/2009]

A young girl sits on a mat in front of the entrance to her hut, making pottery coils, BIRI BIRI. In front of her is the beginning of a pot, about five coils are already built up on top of an old pottery base, KAGYE,  which is used to create the shape. The girl is kneading, TENGUE,  the clay LUDRI. She keeps it moist with water in a metal pot beside her. There is a sequence of this pot being made, unfortunately I've not quite filed it in the right order, but you can see where it goes wrong by the number of coils! The long stick beside her is her walking stick, she had polio as a young child.  (See 2008.78.2.90-101; also 2008.78.1.12). Patti Langton [30/03/2009]

A  side view of a trap, on Jebel Tikye, the tree trunk clearly visible. Small animals, including gazelle and baboon would be caught in these. (See 2008.78.2.96-119, also 2008.78.1.28-35). Patti Langton [11/05/2009]

A young girl sits on the ground, weaving  basket. The fronds (DIRI) are made from the  DURA plant. The basket-maker makes a small square basket base as in the image. She will then then take an old basket, and thread the DIRI fronds of the new base through. The new basket is woven over the old basket for a few centimetres to get the shape, after which she'll detach the old basket and continue to make the new one (see also photos between 2008.78.2.147-157). Patti Langton [19/05/2009]

An image of the new house built by interpreter Andrea in his compound. It isn't quite finished, the thatched roof is not quite done. It is a large rectangular house, quite different from traditional round huts. Andrea is very proud of his house. Patti Langton [12/07/2011]

A set of old stone axe-heads and other stones, laid out on the ground by Surur the rain-maker for Evans-Pritchard to photograph them (although not touch them) from their home in a pot beneath the eaves of his hut, which also contained some of his hair clippings. These stones were called landa loma - stones of Loma, a spiritual connection with rain-making. During rain-making Surur would place these stones along with magical medicines in a pot with rock-pool water and sprinkle to the east where the next day was to arrive from.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) with maize heads and medicines attached, stuck into the ground under a large nilotic shea-butter tree, Vitellaria paradoxa ssp. nilotica, a slow-growing hardwood fruit tree indigenous to northern Uganda and Southern Sudan. During drought this post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake with a carved pot pierced over it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, one of which (to the right) is also surmounted by a carved likeness of the man. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose [cloudy image].

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake (visible to left) with a carved pot pierced over it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, two of which are visible in this image, one with a likeness of the deceased carved at the top. These carvings were understood as a means of honouring the dead but did not have any particular ritual meaning.

A long wooden rain-post (riyak) stuck into the ground under a large tree with a shorter notched post (lingi) for hunting-magic offerings, usually fowl sacrifice. During drought the rain-post was the focus for rain-making rituals involving the sprinkling of durra (Sorghum bicolor) over an assembled crowd by a rain-maker (biriak).

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them); the first a likeness of the deceased, the next clockwise a forked (horn-shaped) post set up by his son-in-law yet tallying his own buffalo kills. The next (only tip visible) is a likeness of the deceased with a tally of two hippo killed, then a forked post tallying six rhino and lastly a forked post tallying five buffalo [cloudy image at centre].

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the east side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela F, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This is the most graceful and most elaborately decorated of all the Quirigua stelae. [...] The graceful arrangement of the feather-work on the upper part of this monument is well worthy of note.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 6) to 9.16.10.0.0, 1 Ahau 3 Zip (Maya calendar), or A.D. 761 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Considered to be one of the great masterpieces of Mesoamerican sculpture, the monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the west side of a carved stone zoomorph known by archaeologists as Zoomorph G, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument is lying on a foundation of three flat stone slabs. For want of a better name my companions in camp were accustomed to call this monument "the armadillo". The arms and legs of the animal portrayed are in much the same position as those on the dragon B, but there are no scrolls on the elbows and knees such as are always found on the dragons. The wrists and ankles are adorned with bracelets and anklets, and the skin is plated with flattened disks or scales.' More recent scholarship dates the zoomorph (also known as Monument 7) to 9.17.15.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 785 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. Identified over the years as various different animals, the carving is now understood by scholars to represent a 'Waterlily Jaguar', with human figures emerging from both ends. The monument was created during the first year of the reign of Sky Xul and records details of the funeral ceremony of his predecessor K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows the west side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela A, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'This monument faces south and stands in line with the stelae C and D in front of the mound which forms the northern boundary of the Great Plaza. Owing to the decayed condition of the stone, the design on the pedestal which supports the figure is somewhat obscure both on the front and on the back of the monument; but in each case parts of the profile of a grotesque mask can be traced.' More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 1) to 9.17.5.0.0 (Maya calendar), or A.D. 775 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat and marked the close of an era in the Maya calendar. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

Portrait of an elderly man (named Lai-iu-ah-tsai-la, better known as Pedro Pino), a former governor of Zuni pueblo during the 1840s and 1850s, sitting, wearing a concha belt and ornaments.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), '[b]eing able to speak the Spanish language[,] he has had many interesting interviews with the army officers and explorers who have visited successively his pueblo, and his name figures prominently in their reports.  He died shortly after his return from the East.'

View of a Zuni man standing beside an eagle cage, a structure made of earth and branches, on top of which sits an eagle.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'people of Zuni possess about seventy-five of these birds which are kept only for their feathers, the bird itself never being elevated to the dignity of an object of worship by the Zunis.  These eagles are kept in stockade cages, and fed on such refuse material as the Indian can provide.  The tail feathers and white downy undergrowth are deemed the most desirable, an area used by the Indians to ornament their persons in sacred dances and ceremonies.'

View of buildings at Nutria pueblo, a Zuni 'outpost or summer resort', with a large decorated pot on the ground in the foreground.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Nutria 'is within the limits of [the Zuni's] reservation, and as the range is a good one and the water of the Nutria springs can be readily taken out for purposes of irrigation, the Zunis repair hither in the spring for the purpose of pasturing their herds or raising small patches of wheat.'

Four Tibetan men in robes standing in a garden, possibly of Dekyi Lingka. An appliquéd canvas is hung behind them and a building is partially visible through vegetation.

Jigme Taring (left), Colonel James Hislop (middle) and another high-ranking official with fur hat sitting, looking towards the camera with tea laid out on a table in front of them. A Tibetan man and woman stand behind them.

Tibetan men seated at a table with stacks of ceremonial food laid out on the table in front of them.  Brocade decorates the back wall and there are paper decorations above it.  There is a brocade hanging from the ceiling with a paper decoration suspended from the  middle of it.  Rai Bahadur Norbu Dhondup sits at the head of the table on a chair decorated with brocade.  He is wearing a ceremonial silk brocade costume and round fur hat.  The other men on the left are all without hats and are guests. The man on the extreme left is wearing spectacles. The food on the table looks like fried bread (kabze) eaten at the time of the New Year.

Taking tea at the Doring house.  Doring's wife is sitting behind a man sitting at the table. Dingja is on the right.  The table is laid with a tablecloth, cups and saucers (European style) and an assortment of cakes and sweets.  A window fitted with glass panes in a diamond pattern is in the background.  Also, there is a group of children in the background (left).

Cuff bracelet, stamped & applied floral motifs, set w/ turquoise & coral
Necklace of red coral, silver, turquoise with pendant
Bison horn spoon with shell and lapis inlay, signed
Church and convent in Santo Domingo
Old Church, Pueblo of Santo Domingo
Modern water vessels from Santa Domingo, Pueblo
Feast Day of Santo Domingo Pueblo

Woven reed cradle hood for girl
Cradle hood for 20/15016 - brown cloth sewn on outside with piece of blue cloth
Ceramic fragment, cylindrical, moulded, buff slip
Pottery disc - used in pottery making

Tray from the collection of G. Nicholson. Coiled, bundle foundation, split stitches, 4x4 plaited start.
Puyallup, Mrs KingGeorge and Nesqually cousins
Grooved straightener, part of arrow-making equipment
White tepary beans with small admixture of dark
Barbed stick for hooking chuck-wallas from between rocks
Dried mesquite, young pods pounded whole and dried
Coiled bowl said to resemble old food bowl
Model 8-stick game, hidden beneath baskets and positions guessed
Model woman's dress, double apron type, of buckskin
Model girl's apron of twisted cloth strips
Basketry exhibit at State Street Bank, 1984
Model seed beater made by Maggie Snyder, from the collection of I.T. Kelly. Close, plain twined.
Water bottle made by Mary Ann Frank, from the collection of I.T. Kelly. Diagonal twined, pigmented and pitched.
Hat from the collection of I.T. Kelly. Diagonal twined, cross warp start, painted design.
Small basket - coiled, design in shades of brown
Woman's apron. Double apron style (2 pieces: front & back) of twined sage bark.
Bottleneck basket with quillwork, from unknown collection. Coiled, bundle foundation, non-interlocking stitches.
Twined circular sifting basket, used largely for mesquite
Panamint display case. Peabody Museum Cases 100 & 99, Rm 15
Winnowing and parching basket made by Susie Shepard, from the collection of J.H. Steward. Open, plain twined.
Food or mush bowl with quill decoration, from the collection of G. Nicholson. Coiled, non-interlocking stitches, spiral start.
Hat with quill decoration from unknown collection. Coiled.
Single-sided, rectangular body stamp made of wood. Design of circles and geometric lines, some forming an X-shape in the centre of the stamp.

Ewey. Open-weave basket with circular rim and hexagonal base. Basket attached to cane rim with twisted string, which extends into a string handle. Previously used; two small breaks in basketry near base; string unravelling in places; some black residue on interior.

Tawa or plaited carrying basket made from cucurito palm. Excess fibres tied in a knot at the base; darker plant fibre used to reinforce the rim and form a handle which is tied onto the rim at two points.
Half of a gourd, with a broadly oval shaped body and a black coated inner surface. Used for eating and drinking.
Ya'ara pujpe. Stool made from a tortoise shell.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural geometric pattern with crosses. Small loop of fibre attached to the cane.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural with six rows of centipede motifs within squares. Thin loop of fibre attached to the frame.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural geometric pattern with two central rows of lizard motifs within squares.

Wapa. A small, shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited black and natural geometric pattern with four central lizard motifs within squares. Small loop of fibre attached to the cane.
Panayo. Ear piercing instrument. Coloured red for piercing the ears of females. Formed of sharpened, crossed skewers with diamond of woven wool in the centre.
Rush basket made of coiled fibre in concentric circles with a woven handle; handle is detached at one end.
Wooden slat body armour in 2 parts, with painted geometric designs and small faces carved in a line round the centre.
Container made from a length of bamboo cut off below joint at one end to create a base for the cylinder. Large split down one long side.
Fan made of large toucan feathers, which are black with white tips. Feathers are connected near base with two wooden pieces. Used to fan fires.

Dancing belt worn around the waist, with pieces of large snail shells hung from red and white cloth waist band on grass strings. Strings are decorated with black seeds, fish bones, some bird bones and few pieces of black plastic.
Fibrous lengths of plant tied in a knot and bundled. Fibres grow on trees and are used in weaving. Used by both sexes.
Abilla, large seed pod. Purgative medicine, taken grated.

Chikai. Beaded dance girdle or belt. Design of red triangles on a white background. Glass beads are strung on twisted vegetable fibres between two lengths of cotton-wrapped cane with cotton ties extensions knotted together and presumably used for fastening. Strings of beads are tangled and there are many loose strings which have become detached from the cane ends.

Watch strap, made by Irina Nutti, composed of de-haired reindeer leather (sisti), yellow woollen textile, and pewter thread. Base is a rectangular band of leather with rounded corners. Edges of the leather are turned over a smaller band of yellow woollen textile, sewn with waxed nylon thread, and decorated with geometric designs in pewter thread. Back has two slits, through which a narrower leather strip is passed; one end has five small perforations, other end has a metal buckle, possibly of nickel.

Tungpaw(?). Woman’s long-sleeved, wrap dress or robe of black velvet, lined with cotton or synthetic black fabric; open to side with buttons along top right. Round collar with orange zigzag beaded decoration and pink cotton lining. Garment edges on both sides decorated with band of geometric motifs in orange, yellow, green, white and black beads and further row of stitched aluminium discs with aluminium chain above. Centre and reverse front decorated with black and blue velvet appliquéd beaded butterfly at centre, with anthropomorphic figures flanked by snakes, above and below. Cuffs and right side of chest appliquéd with velvet panels of repeated beaded anthropomorphic figures with aluminium discs and chain below.

Ibuk. Round neck, long sleeved jacket of blue velvet, decorated with anthropomorphic and zoomorphic figures in orange, yellow, green and white glass beads. Centre front appliquéd with black velvet panels with rows of beaded anthropomorphic heads, arms raised; seven shell buttons with yellow, red and green plaited synthetic wool loops. Semicircular appliqué collar on reverse with three beaded snake-like figures intersected by beaded faces and enclosed by geometric bands containing sequins; aluminium chain stitched below collar. Large appliqué tiger, two butterflies and further winged figure at centre reverse. Panels of beaded anthropomorphic figures along bottom edge with snake motifs either side. Appliqué sleeve panels depict snake-like figure, butterfly and snake; cuff panels of foliate motifs containing sequins with geometric bands above and below. Metal discs stitched along beadwork edges. Blue synthetic cloth lining.
Square teapot 'in the shape of a bell', with the stamps giving the name of the maker on the base of the pot, under the lid and at the base of the handle. Teapot made of dark brown clay.
One of ten paintings of Manipuri tribesmen of Assam, painted by a Manipuri artist. Kuki woman. Forms a pair with 1951.764.9.
Phremphun. Necklace; Religious beads made of seeds from a tree. May be worn as a necklace as part of Pa-chyu costume.

A cream coloured square cloth made of four strips of woven textile, possibly nettle, stitched together with black thread. The cloth has been woven with raised ribs along the short width of the panels; the cloth has been hemmed along two edges. Twisted piece of plant fibre found with cloth.

Rhengaa. Carrying bag part of traditional Tamu Gurung man's costume, called Rhengaa, also used by pa-chyu Shaman. Made of nettle fibre. The bag is worn around shoulders, with the pouch for carrying hanging at the back and sides.

Chhyonlen. Pair of brass cymbals of a type used by Pa-chyu and Khhlyprin shamans and lamas. Those of the Khhlyprin may be larger. In the past ancestors used two stones instead of cymbals. The cymbals are the second friend of the drum, played by the Shaman's assistant to accompany the drum. Made by case of brass makers Phahde Khhle who live in city; Good

Chyhasun. Spirit Catcher. A bird's head (chhahkra) and beak (chyhasun) of a saras used to help 1993.42 to collect the spirits. Used by Pa-chyu shaman. The bird has to be trapped on a ' special' day. N.B. It is important that the birds 1993.44-46 are all different. Each obtained on a different ' special' day as determined by astrology.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Khus Bahadur, a Limbu man.

Metal bracelet with glass beads and a hook and eye fastening. Triangular end plates and a central spacer plate supporting two lengths of three chains; chain links made up of circular discs with two rings attached to each sides; blue and red glass seed beads set into the end and spacer plates with filigree decoration.

Pair of black leather boots with thick composite sole. Lined with blue cloth, with a blue silk band around the top of the opening; cream leather piping along seams and curvilinear embroidery at the heel in white and pink; cream, green and pink braided cord around top of sole which consists of layers of leather and cloth; bottom of sole is concave.
Bös. Orange silk sash with design in the weft.

Pleated apron of white cotton. Square shaped with a rounded hem; formed of six panels with twelve pleats, decorated with vertical blue stitching along each pleat of varying lengths, and along the sides. Tied with a blue waist band that ends in a point, from which a thinner blue band projects which also ends in a point. On the interior of the hem is a rectangular panel stitched with blue thread.

Pair of cotton shoes with leather soles, decorated with embroidery. Uppers of blue cotton, lined with undyed cotton and embroidered with lines of black stitching; around the opening is a wide band of embroidered and woven red silk, with green and red at the toe; composite soles made layers of leather with additional thin wedges at the heel; interior of sole is unlined. Paper secured around silk embroidery with blue tacking stitches.
A rectangular piece of yellow bark with an ink drawing of a stick carrying two jars at either end, used as a demand for honey.
Brass pendants worn in a string around the waist by unmarried Galo and Minyong girls. Decorated with concentric circles crossed with two twisted ropes of bronze.
A woman's skirt made from a rectangular piece of thick white cotton textile woven with thin blue stripes, stitched together into a tube.

Blue skirt. The skirt is pleated with a white floral pattern. There is a panel of checked red fabric sewn to one side and the waistband, and the hem is decorated with embroidery in red, green, and yellow.

Ãepiec. Woman's cap made of white fabric with multicoloured embroidered and cross-stitched decorations. The back has cross-stitched decorations of flowers and patterns. A woven panel with embroidered floral decorations and lace is sewn to the front.
White apron. The apron is pleated with woven decorations in red, pink, and black. The bottom is black with embroidered letters and embroidered decoration on the hem.
Beige table cloth with Hardanger-style embroidery.
A piece of cloth with embroidered patterns in red, blue, yellow, green, purple, pink, and blue. Possibly a piece of an unfinished cap.

A doll made of a strip of trimmed fur with pieces of green, yellow, red, and blue fabric sewn to the back and the bottom. The head of the doll is made of the top half of a bird's beak with part of the skin of the bird's head attached to the fur.
Pin made of blackthorn wood, trimmed and fried in fat, made by Leviathon Pickett. One terminal tapers to a point, the other is flat. Natural knots present on the wood.

Tamata. Votive offering. Representation of a head and neck, modelled in pale green wax, black-eyed beans represent the eyes. The hair is shoulder length with a patch of pink colour at the back of the head. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head, suggesting a point of suspension.
Tamata. Votive offering of an eye cut out of sheet silver. Depiction of eye has been engraved on one side. There is a semicircular tab and hole at the top for the attachment of a pin.

Tamata. Votive offering. Representation of an arm, stamped on thin, silver sheet to produce a slightly raised design. Incised detail around outline. The arm is bent at a right-angle. There is a semicircular tab and hole on the upper part of the arm for the attachment of a pin.

Sacred bamboo flute covered for most of its length, except mouth-hole, with plaited cane sleeves, coloured blackish red. Black cassowary feathers attached round coiled cane work flange at base and at approximately mid-length. Flute ornament in shape of a pig's head with fish's body and tail projecting above end of bamboo.

A woman's one-piece wooden paddle that has been shortened, the shaft end now a rough point. Narrow lanceolate blade which is carved on its lower half, either side of a mid-rib, with ovoid ' eyes' and plain and toothed crescent curves. Shaft top carved with design of zigzag infilled ovoids between curved verticals, and a zigzag band underneath.

Representation - Narrow openwork wooden board, carved with distinct face and 4 hook prongs in each of 2 windows near base. Toothed top with central boss, a point with raised oval ' eyes' . Ovoid face set in side curves with hook eyes and long nose ridge pierced with 4 strutted tear shapes. Nose-ridge continues down to ' chest' area. Spiral or hook curve cheek marks circule out from the nose. Mouth also has side curves. Main body panel has two bird's heads with vertically interlocking beaks in centre. Two other bird's beaks point straight out from nose ridge near top of body panel. Rest of panel filled with pierced ' lobefaces' . Base carved with spirals or hook curves, corners rounded and small butt in centre of bottom edge. No face at rear. Traces of red, black & white paint, thickest on face, especially the white background. Rough overcoiled cane loop attached through piercings in top of nose ridge. Cracked with pieces missing, colours faded. Original accession notes: " Large openwork carving representing the face of the sago-beetle (PANANGUN). These objects are said to be no longer made (? ceased to be made before white contact). They are kept in dwelling houses but I do not know their significance. From the arrangement of the bottom of the plank I judge they are a type of ceremonial hook probably " altars" of some kind. No other specimens were seen in the houses." Poor

Lime gourd. Broad curved gourd, with oval cross-section. Upper half incised with design of 2 large faces with smaller faces inset in the nose area. Infilled with charcoal. Two other faces upside down between the large faces at bottom. Plain fringe at base. At top oval rings in wavy lines and scalloped border. Said to have been manufactured by Tshambuli. Original accession notes: " Ornamented with faces which the Iatmul describe as WINDSHIMBU - spirits which live in trees and occasionally act as shamanic spirits possessing men and are impersonated by the initiates when water-drums are shown to novices. WINDSHIMBU are also identified with flutes, which are in myth said to be derived from the cut-off penis of WINDSHIMBU. This type of ornamentation of lime-gourds is practised among the Iatmul and (?) in Tshambuli. I do not know where it originated. The word WINDSHIMBU is probably etymologically connected with UNDUMBU (= ghosts). But at the present time these two types of spiritual being are clearly discriminated." Good
Beater for gong. Stick with rounded base and flattened pointed tip with toothed section and two small round lugs above the narrower handle section. No colouring or surface carving.

A Nggwail representation which may represent a shamanic spirit, Lamwail. A full-length wooden figure with large ovoid head fringed with human hair, border covered in red gum studded with nassa and cowrie shells, and along forehead conus shells.

Long narrow full-length figure with bird on its back carved in a pale hard wood. Has two loop slots to take pole in front. Traces of black paint on man's face and arms. Feet, ankles and base painted black, with some red paint on the side of the right leg and the front side of the bottom loop slot. Rough carving, with chisel marks still visible. Head ovoid with raised cap, oval ring and dot eyes, raised crescent mouth, pierced club nose with twist of palm knotted through it. Narrow double pierced ears, very long neck. Arms hang to the sides of the elongated trunk and are joined to it at the elbow by the second loop slat. Hands rest above the thighs with fingers carved, but of a rough round outline. Hollow belly with loop slat across it. Male genitals prominent. Legs bent slightly at the knees where the other loop slat is, and the stump feet rest on the top of the triangular pointed base which has a large central groove. Bird has lug in wattle or pouch position on underside of neck. 8 lugs down bird's back, and toothed curve design incised lightly on bird's folded wings with a face at the top of each wing. Below the bird's tail is a second bracket reaching to the bottom of the man's trunk. Bird's legs bent with talons carved. Feet rest on back of man's head. Bird has knob eyes, knob ears and a plain curved beak. Fibre ear and nose rings for human figure. Original accession notes: " A recent carving, bored to fix on a pole, representing a man NDO and a WAWI (a species of bird). This specimen was not regarded seriously, but ' it would have had to be hidden if it had been old' ." Fair
Head made of pith-like wood. It has human hair stuck in the forehead and is decorated with white paint and black lines

Arrow with two blackened wood points, bound at their base with cane. One point has prominent alternate side barbs, widely spaced; the other has small equal and opposite side barbs. No foreshaft. Shaft binding of coiled and diagonally crossed cane. Tapering bamboo shaft.

Wide dish on pedestal foot with hammerhead rim and pierced lug on rim. Decorated in six sections alternating between dark maroon slip and pale/dark pink patterns: Dar, Thebana and Jerida (the horse, the fly, the palm leaf).
Pot of burnished red ware. Slightly everted rim, tall and narrow neck, rounded body and flat base. Decorated at central body with horizontal band of chevrons, incised with pointed stick.

Black pottery pipe bowl with polished surface. Sharp elbow with cylindrical stem and flared bowl. The edge of the bowl slightly bevelled and decorated with short grooved lines; a light groove running round the top of the stem. Small fragment of stem broken off and missing.
Small burnished pot with a flat base, globular body and a short narrow neck with slightly everted rim. Decorated with four incised horizontal lines and multiple hanging triangles.

A large rectangular cloth of cream cotton, possibly a body cloth. It is made from two large rectangles of cream cotton cloth that have been folded lengthways and sewn together.  Towards one end, the cloth is woven with thick red stripes and one thick blue stripe; the is geometric embroidery in dark blue between the red stripes, and thin double stripes running towards the edge.

Male funerary ornament. Two woollen bobbles or pom-poms, one green with magenta centre, one magenta with green centre, ornamented with two sets of two grey beads, probably glass, connected by length of black woollen twine.

An over skirt made from thin, loosely woven cotton with stripes of metal thread woven through, a red cotton waistband and an embellished hem. The hem is made of a band of red cotton with a trim of black velvet along the top, green silk along with bottom and metallic gold in the centre; the black and green trims are embellished with metal sequins and clear glass beads; the gold band is embellished with round mirrors set in gold repoussé metal frames and metal sequins and clear glass beads; the bottom edge of the hem is lined with silver glass beads and metal sequins.

T-shaped belt. Waist band of red felt with central, woven gold band decorated with central row of circular mirrors, with gold-coloured metal serrated surrounds, sewn with white cotton and rows of silver-coloured sequins with small metal spirals at centre. Wide sash of red felt with two rows of mirrors and same decoration as waist band. Trapezoid sash base with two diamond-shaped, serrated mirrors; rows of vertical, thin, gold wrapped tubes, with green velvet top and bottom and central band of red felt decorated with metal sequins; twisted silver thread tassels at base and metal trim on sides. Reverse lined with red cotton and green silk, stitched on with black and white cotton.

Pennanular gilded brass armlet. Made from sheet metal, rolled over at the edges to create a hollow tubular shape; protruding pyramidal forms around the outer surface; gilded on the outer surface. One of four armlets, 1944.22.6.13-16.
Waist-cloth worn by men. Long, rectangular strip of undyed woven cloth; decorated at both ends with wide bands of red and blue woven geometric patterns; short fringe at both ends.

Mala. White, blue and yellow bead necklace. The ends and the central motif of the necklace have white and yellow beads arranged into flower shapes, with blue beads around them. At the sides of the necklace, white beads are arranged into three strands. Worn by young men and women.

Nootiet, quiver (.1) of bamboo, cylindrical, covered with black leather with a leather lid attached by a leather shoulder-strap. Supetiat, arrows (.2-8) have feather fletchings, one with a wooden tip, five metal and one missing the tip. (.9-11) are fragments of arrows.
A knife or fleam. The blade is thin with a curved cutting edge, it is set into a wooden stick and secured with hide binding. Used for the blood letting of goats.
Simple bow with sinew string. Wooden bow with circular cross-section tapering towards either end; strip of leather around one end to prevent the string from slipping.

Quiver made from bamboo and leather containing 18 poisoned arrows. Hollow cylindrical quiver with leather base and removable cap; vertical strips of leather held in place by loops; handle made from a wide strip of leather; one porcupine quill in the leather binding. 18 notched arrows of cane, some with feather fletching. Some leather strips broken.

A square bag made of dark blue cotton woven with vertical and embroidered with horizontal stripes in orange and white. It has a long wide strap that forms the sides of the bag, and front and back panels attached with orange and white threads. There are tassels at the bottom two corners, the top edges bound with orange threads.

A square bag made of white cotton woven with vertical red and black stripes, embroidered with horizontal stripes in red and green wool. It has a long wide strap that forms the sides of the bag. There is fringing at the bottom two corners.

A wooden tobacco box with a hinged lid. It is roughly rectangular in shape, but the two shorter edges are rounded and convex. The lid is decorated with an incised picture of a man and a woman; the man seems to be wearing a uniform and lapels. The figures are coloured with black, green, and red pigment, and there are green and red spiralled banners on each side, and a circular design in the middle. There is a band of decoration around the sides of the box, and a picture of a man wearing a suit on the bottom. The man is wearing a red hat, and is holding a red and green plant; there are also plants in the upper left and bottom right corner.

Staff comprising a horn handle carved in the form of a S-shaped sea animal, possibly a fish, attached with two metal nails to a long, narrow, curved wooden shaft with a bulbous end. The horn animal is decorated with incised patterns of semicircles and dots, and has a slit mouth with a tongue stained with red pigment.
Mole's paw amulet in metal fitting with suspension loop.
A pair of navy blue wool leggings, with a brown cotton braid trim. They have a tab with a beige and brown cords attached at the top, and brass metal hook and eye fastenings at the ankles.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of navy, blue, brown and maroon. Tied together.

Shirt - A: two long shirts or " kameushu" of cotton print in white and grey check. Pleat on chest and in front of skirt. For everyday use. B: fine, white, linen shirt. More fully pleated in front. For festive occasions. All worn by men

A necklace consisting of glass beads stitched onto a cloth backing. The cloth is rectangular with four tabs. The beads consist of lines of blue, white and red along the top; the tabs have central stripes of white and blue, and are outlined with rows of red, white and black. Loops of beads at one end and glass button at the other.

Latuka helmet with ostrich plumes. The foundation of the helmet is make from hair and fibre covered with multiple sheets of brass. At the top of the helmet are several large ostrich feathers, one loose.

Composite, side-blown horn or trumpet, made from two horns. The top half is antelope horn, loosely coiled in shape, with an oval blow-hole in the side close to the top. Holes have been made around the bottom rim of the antelope horn, which have been used to stitch the upper horn to the cow horn, which forms the flared bell of the instrument. The join between the two horns has been bound with strips of hide, and there is a woven band of leather around the end of the bell.

Spear, with small, leaf-shaped, socketed iron blade with central midrib. Long shaft tapers towards the end. The surface of the shaft is slightly even due to the natural grain of the wood. The shaft has been decorated with black pigment applied in a swirling, abstract design.
A men's bracelet. Made from two warthog tusks, joined together by hide wrapped around the ends and stitched together with fibre.
Girdle made of white and black beads and carved minosa wood. Single strand of white beads, which splits into two on either side; this is attached to the wooden beads. Girdle is tied at one end.
An armlet made from two warthog tusks, joined together by hide wrapped around the ends and stitched together with fibre.
Ornament to be worn in the hair. Circular disc of leather with a spiral of glass beads stitched to it; translucent red, striped pink white and green, and opaque white beads.

Throwing spear with a wooden shaft and metal spearhead. The blade is leaf shaped with a midrib; split socket with a circular cross-section. The shaft has a circular cross-section and terminates with a metal ferrule. There is a ring of hide around the shaft near the ferrule.

Cup or ladle with handle. Hollowed sphere of wood with a cylindrical handle tapering towards one end and looped back on itself; stained dark red with an area of lighter red at the thin end of the handle.

Shield made of wood and cane with hide rim. Wooden pointed-oval structure with central ridge, v-shaped cross-section and central conical boss; covered with woven cane strips in two colours and a strip of hair covered hide affixed around rim; handle made from three wooden arches inserted into shield and covered with woven cane strips.
Spear. Rounded iron head with sharply tapering point, mid-rib and areas of dark pigmentation either side. Wooden shaft. Iron ferrule detached and missing.

A globular pot with an everted rim and four narrow, cylindrical legs attached at the base. The outer body of the vessel has a reflective, dark grey glaze; likely derived from graphite. The legs are red in colour. Used for roasting coffee.

A milk pot with a narrow, everted rim, a tapering neck, globular body and rounded base.  The outer body of the vessel has a reflective, dark grey glaze; likely derived from graphite. Decorated at the base of the neck with a raised band marked with intersecting lines in a chevron style pattern. The base is decorated with a circle filled with linear and zigzag patterns.
